title: Existence of strings without simple optimal hypotheses
formal:
For every polynomial sampling budget, do infinitely many lengths contain a string with no simple optimal statistical hypothesis, when its reference description is allowed a larger polynomial time budget?

The selected unconditional proposition is
\[
\forall U\in\mathcal U\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\exists d\in\mathbb N_{>c}\
\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge N}\quad
\operatorname{Bad}_U(c,d,n).
\]
Here \(\mathcal U\) is the explicitly defined class of polynomially universal finite machines below. Write
\[
\begin{split}
\operatorname{Bad}_U(c,d,n)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n\ \forall\mu\in\mathcal D_n\quad
\bigl[
&\operatorname{Simple}_U(\mu;n^c,c\log_2 n)\\
&\Longrightarrow\
\mu(x)\le n^{-c}2^{-C_U^{n^d}(x)}
\bigr].
\end{split}
\]
The set \(\mathcal D_n\) consists of rational probability distributions on \(n\)-bit strings. Simplicity requires an exact sampler with description length strictly less than \(c\log_2 n\), halting within \(n^c\) steps on every choice of its fair random bits. The quantity \(C_U^{n^d}(x)\) is the length of a shortest deterministic description producing \(x\) within \(n^d\) steps. Optimality requires the strict reverse likelihood inequality, so the displayed weak inequality expresses its failure.

The exponent \(d\) may depend on \(U,c\), but must be chosen before the length threshold \(N\), the witness length \(n\), and the string \(x\). The same exponent \(c\) sets the sampling time, logarithmic description budget and inverse-polynomial likelihood slack. No algorithm generating the witness strings is required.

This is the explicitly selected editorial formulation of the source question. The original Question 3 does not state this quantifier order or tie these three budgets to one exponent, and its presentation also invites conditional results. The target here is the displayed unconditional proposition, not a claim that the source already states exactly this variant.
why: This target asks whether computation limits can create an intrinsic gap between descriptions of individual data and simple probabilistic models of that data. It concerns existence of explanatory models, beyond the success of one model-selection or learning algorithm. A resolution would clarify how exact randomized sampling and time-bounded algorithmic information constrain statistical explanation. The selected asymptotic regime makes this structural question precise while leaving its scientific status separate from the editorial choice.

sentences: The question asks whether some binary strings lack every simple probabilistic explanation satisfying a specified time-bounded likelihood comparison.
For each polynomial sampling budget, a simple explanation must be sampled exactly by a logarithmically short randomized program that halts within that budget on every random choice.
The selected target permits a larger polynomial time bound for describing the string and asks for strings without such explanations at infinitely many lengths.
This is an explicit unconditional editorial formulation because the source did not fix the order of its polynomial time bounds.
A complete Lean answer must prove the quantified existence statement or its full negation, clarifying how computational limits constrain statistical explanations of individual data.

definitions:
A binary string is a finite sequence of symbols from \(\{0,1\}\); \(|x|\) denotes its length and \(\Lambda\) the empty string. All logarithms have base two. For \(n\ge2\), define
\[
\mathcal D_n=
\left\{\mu:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}:
\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}^n}\mu(z)=1\right\}.
\]
A hypothesis is a mathematical distribution \(\mu\in\mathcal D_n\). Values in likelihood inequalities are regarded as real numbers. The distribution is not supplied as an oracle to a program, and the definition does not require efficient computation of its point probabilities.

Use the following explicit completion of the source's one-tape machine convention. A deterministic machine has a finite set of control states, a designated initial state and halt state, and one tape with cells indexed by the integers and alphabet \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), where \(\square\) is blank. On the triple of binary arguments \((p,y,r)\), the tape initially contains \(p\#y\#r\#\) starting at cell zero and is blank elsewhere. The head starts at cell zero, and a separate write-only binary output stream is empty. Each nonhalting transition reads the current state and symbol, writes one tape symbol, moves the head by \(-1,0\), or \(1\), changes the state, and appends either no bit or one bit to the output stream. The transition table is finite, deterministic, and defined on every nonhalting state and tape symbol. The stream cannot be read. Entering the halt state returns exactly the emitted binary string. A nonhalting computation has undefined output.

One transition costs one step, including transitions emitting output. Initial input placement is not charged. Space is the number of distinct tape cells visited by the head, including its initial cell. The finite transition table is the machine's entire fixed control; it receives no oracle, advice or additional real-valued parameter. All input strings, programs and random strings are finite.

Let \(\mathcal U\) be the class of machines in this convention satisfying the following polynomial universality property. For every machine \(V\) in the same convention, there are integers \(a,b,k\ge1\) such that
\[
\forall p\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ \exists q\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\quad
|q|\le |p|+b
\]
and \(U(q,y,r)=V(p,y,r)\) as partial functions for every pair of binary strings \(y,r\). The same \(q\) must work for all \(y,r\). Whenever the latter computation halts in \(s\) steps using \(h\) tape cells, the former halts in at most
\[
a(1+|y|+|r|+s)^k
\]
steps and uses at most
\[
a(1+|y|+|r|+h)^k
\]
tape cells. The constants may depend on \(U,V\), but not on \(p,y,r\); the translated program \(q\) may depend on \(p\). Equality as partial functions includes agreement on divergence. This is the usual constant-description-overhead, polynomial-resource universality condition, and the class is nonempty. No prefix-free restriction is imposed on programs. Quantifying over this defined class avoids leaving an unspecified universal transition table as a parameter of the question.

For an integer \(t\ge0\), define plain time-bounded description complexity by
\[
C_U^t(x)=
\min\{|p|:U(p,\Lambda,\Lambda)
\text{ halts within }t\text{ steps with output }x\}.
\]
If the set is empty, define \(C_U^t(x)=+\infty\) and \(2^{-\infty}=0\). This is complexity of producing the string, rather than recognizing it, and is plain rather than prefix complexity.

A randomized description is a pair \((p,m)\), where \(p\) is a binary program and \(m\ge1\) is an integer. Independently choose \(m\) fair bits, giving each \(r\in\{0,1\}^m\) probability \(2^{-m}\), and execute \(U(p,\Lambda,r)\). The charged description length is the real number
\[
\ell(p,m)=|p|+\log_2 m,
\]
as in the source; it is not the bit length of a self-delimiting encoding of the pair. The random-string choice and initial placement specify the probability experiment. Time counts the subsequent machine transitions and must be bounded on every one of the finitely many random strings. Requiring \(m\ge1\) makes \(\log_2 m\) defined; a bit may be unused.

The pair samples \(\mu\in\mathcal D_n\) within \(t_0\) steps when every run on \(r\in\{0,1\}^m\) halts within \(t_0\), outputs a string in \(\{0,1\}^n\), and satisfies
\[
\forall z\in\{0,1\}^n\quad
\mu(z)=2^{-m}
\left|\{r\in\{0,1\}^m:U(p,\Lambda,r)=z\}\right|.
\]
Here the vertical bars on the set denote its cardinality. Sampling is exact and total on all random strings, with no failure symbol. Such samplers realize dyadic probabilities; the broader hypothesis domain is still all rational distributions. No requirement to evaluate \(\mu(z)\) efficiently is added.

For \(t_0\in\mathbb N\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the predicate \(\operatorname{Simple}_U(\mu;t_0,\alpha)\) means that some pair samples \(\mu\) within \(t_0\) steps and has \(\ell(p,m)<\alpha\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), define
\[
\operatorname{Optimal}_U(\mu,x;t,\varepsilon)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mu(x)>\varepsilon\,2^{-C_U^t(x)}.
\]
The strict inequality follows the source's Definition 11. In the target, \(t_0=n^c\), \(\alpha=c\log_2 n\), \(t=n^d\), and \(\varepsilon=n^{-c}\). There are no suppressed multiplicative constants or further asymptotic terms in these predicates. Each candidate distribution and sampler may depend on the particular string and length; the assertion ranges over all of them within the stated budgets. Infinitely many lengths means precisely that for every integer \(N\ge2\) a witnessing integer \(n\ge N\) exists.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed unconditional proposition or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must prove that for every \(U\in\mathcal U\) and integer \(c\ge2\), some fixed integer \(d>c\) has witnessing strings at arbitrarily large lengths. At each witnessing length, the same string \(x\) must satisfy the likelihood upper bound for every distribution having any qualifying exact sampler. The proof need not construct these strings by one effective procedure.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists U\in\mathcal U\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\forall d\in\mathbb N_{>c}\
\exists N\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge N}\quad
\neg\operatorname{Bad}_U(c,d,n).
\]
Equivalently, for every such \(d\), after its permitted threshold \(N\), one must prove
\[
\forall n\ge N\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n\
\exists\mu\in\mathcal D_n\quad
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{Simple}_U(\mu;n^c,c\log_2 n),\\
\mu(x)>n^{-c}2^{-C_U^{n^d}(x)}.
\end{cases}
\]
The distribution and sampler may depend on \(n,x,d\), while the same fixed \(c\) bounds their sampling time and description length. The threshold \(N\) may depend on \(d\). This negation requires existence of the hypotheses with these budgets; it does not require a uniform algorithm finding them from \(x\).

Both directions must use the specified finite-machine, description and probability conventions, and prove all of the stated quantifiers. Restricting a positive nonexistence result to uniform distributions on sets, efficiently evaluable probabilities or a chosen sampler family does not cover the full hypothesis class. A theorem about the distinct source notions of acceptable or plausible hypotheses is insufficient unless it establishes the defined optimality assertion. A result depending on an additional unproved complexity assumption is conditional progress, not a proof of this unconditional proposition or its negation. This is an exact existence question; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not replace its likelihood comparisons or quantifiers.

context_blocks.text: The original paper distinguishes acceptable, plausible and optimal hypotheses under computational limits. Question 3 asks about strings lacking simple optimal hypotheses; it does not fix how the polynomial time bounds depend on one another.

This card adopts an explicit unconditional variant: for each sampler exponent \(c\), the reference-description exponent \(d>c\) may depend on \(c\), and strings without a qualifying optimal hypothesis must occur at infinitely many lengths. This specified regime is an editorial choice, not an equivalence attributed to the source.

The relative time budgets matter. The source establishes existence of simple optimal hypotheses when the sampler receives sufficiently more time than the reference description, so those budgets cannot be omitted or reversed without changing the question.

The official presentation asks under which assumptions such strings exist. The present target is unconditional; the presentation does not certify this precise quantified variant as an established conjecture.

The 2018 follow-up studies polynomial-time prediction in indexed families of distributions using another optimality definition. Its prediction-neighborhood comparisons do not resolve the selected finite-string existence statement.

The 2024 paper explicitly distinguishes its uncomputable predictor from an effective prediction algorithm. This prevents its unbounded-computation guarantee from being read as a polynomial-time resolution here.

Actual publisher source cached as hypothesis-simple-ccc2017.pdf/.txt was reread at PDF pp. 4–5, 7–8, 11 and 14. §2 specifies universal one-tape computation with constant program overhead and polynomial time and space simulation overhead; randomized descriptions are pairs (p,m), charged |p| + log m, with worst-case running time over all equally likely m-bit random strings. Definition 4 requires exact total sampling; Definition 11 uses a strict greater-than likelihood comparison. The raw Question 3 is on printed p. 17:11 and lacks the adopted asymptotic quantifier order.

The selected parameterization t0 = n^c, alpha = c log_2 n, t = n^d, epsilon = n^(-c), c >= 2, forall c exists d > c, infinitely many n, is explicitly editorial. The source supplies the notions, polynomial/logarithmic setting and the warning about relative time budgets, but does not state this complete combination. No claim of source equivalence is made. No complexity assumption is part of the target. Source slides inviting conditional results are preserved as distinct context.

Do not copy the exists-d/forall-c order from the source theorem about acceptable or plausible explanations. For a fixed reference time t = n^d, Proposition 14 and its proof supply each string a sampler with polynomial(n+t) time and logarithmic(n+t) description. A sufficiently large c absorbs those budgets. Thus the copied opposite order would create a false target rather than faithfully specify Question 3. The approved order avoids that particular triviality but is not thereby proved open.

Boundary audit: Definition 11 has strict >. Proposition 14 is stated with epsilon = 1, whereas the proof in §5.6 establishes probability at least 2^(-C^t(x)); the displayed talk comparison is also non-strict. The public known-result context and audit rely only on inverse-polynomial epsilon < 1, where the proof bound gives the required strict inequality. No stronger epsilon = 1 statement or silent repair of the original formula is imported.

The original source gives a one-tape machine with three binary arguments but does not spell out tape layout or returned-output encoding. The selected concrete transducer convention uses p#y#r# on one two-way tape and charges every emitted output bit. This avoids free output from an arbitrarily long prefilled program, which would conflict with a universality time bound omitting |p|. Fixed alphabet, head, initial configuration, output, halting, divergence, time and visited-cell space conventions are explicit. Ordinary finite transducer conventions of this kind admit universal simulation with constant description overhead and fixed polynomial resource overhead. All-machine quantification makes the formal target independent of an unspecified transition table.

Machine-invariance audit: write A_U for the selected forall-c/exists-d proposition with a fixed U. Suppose A_U holds and V is another member of the stated class. Fix V’s sampler exponent c. Any V-simple description has m < n^c because |p| + log_2 m < c log_2 n. Simulating its program on U adds a fixed b_1 to program length and costs at most a fixed polynomial in m+n^c. Choose an integer C > c sufficiently large so that, for all sufficiently large n, every such sampler becomes U-simple at budgets n^C and C log_2 n. Apply A_U at C to get D > C. The converse U-to-V simulation, now on deterministic descriptions with empty other inputs, gives for a sufficiently large integer d > c the inequality C_V^(n^d)(x) <= C_U^(n^D)(x) + b_2 whenever the latter is finite, for all sufficiently large n. Both simulation constants are independent of c,D,n and x once U,V are fixed.

Continuing that audit, each V-simple distribution on a U-witness x satisfies mu(x) <= n^(-C) 2^(-C_U^(n^D)(x)) <= 2^(b_2) n^(-C) 2^(-C_V^(n^d)(x)) <= n^(-c) 2^(-C_V^(n^d)(x)) after increasing the length threshold. If the U complexity is infinite, its zero exponential already forces mu(x)=0; if it is finite, the simulated V description exists. Removing finitely many lengths preserves infinitely many witnesses. Therefore A_U implies A_V, and symmetry gives equivalence. Since ordinary universal simulation supplies at least one machine in the class, forall U is equivalent to fixing any one of these universal machines. This is a model-equivalence check, not a proposed approach to solving A.

The source leaves log 0 undefined. The selected convention requires m >= 1 and permits a dummy unused fair bit, so deterministic samplers remain possible. Time is the maximum of U execution times after the random string is supplied, as in the source. Charging m additional coin-preparation steps would change sampler costs only by a polynomial absorbed by the same exponent transfer, because the length budget implies m < n^c. Description length is the real value |p|+log_2 m, not a guessed binary pair encoding. Samplers must halt and output an n-bit string on every coin string; finite support, dyadic probabilities and exact equality are explicit.

Hypotheses are all rational distributions on strings of one fixed length. Simplicity is existential exact sampling, so realized hypotheses are dyadic; no efficient point-probability evaluator is demanded. The source explicitly calls out that different simplicity requirement separately for Theorem 18. Restricting to efficiently evaluable distributions, uniform distributions on sets or a particular sampler family would weaken the positive impossibility requirement and is not the selected target.

The complete negation is exists U exists c forall d > c exists N forall n >= N forall x exists a simple optimal mu. Its threshold may depend on d, and its hypotheses and samplers may depend on n,x,d. There is no effective constructor requirement on the negation and no computable witness-sequence requirement on the positive statement. The weak failure inequality <= is the exact complement of strict optimality >, including the defined infinite-complexity case.
